title: A peephole and a mirror taught the Renaissance to paint depth
body: Painters had long shown distant things smaller, but without a consistent system. Between about 1415 and 1420, the Florentine architect Filippo Brunelleschi, later famous for the dome of Florence Cathedral, showed how to do it exactly: lines running straight away from the viewer all meet at one vanishing point on the horizon. He tested it with a painted panel, a peephole and a mirror, and soon artists such as Masaccio and Donatello were using his method.

slides.alt: Animation in fresco colours: a side-view diagram shows an eye behind a painted panel, looking through a hole at the Florence Baptistery, then at the painting in a raised mirror. Then a tiled floor is built: a horizon, a vanishing point, lines running to it, rows crowding closer.

slides.prompt: You are looking down from 3 m. Drag the people around the floor, then lower your eye until all their heads touch the horizon.
slides.takeaway: Every floor line runs to one vanishing point on the horizon, and anything as tall as your eye reaches the horizon however far away: Alberti’s similar triangles, size divided by distance.

slides.heading: The painted panel
slides.text: Brunelleschi painted the Baptistery as seen from the doorway of Florence Cathedral, then made a small hole through the panel. You looked through it from behind; a raised mirror swapped the real view for the painted one.

events.text: Masolino: earliest surviving consistent vanishing point
Masaccio’s Holy Trinity, at eye level
Alberti explains it in De pictura

slides.heading: Writing the rules
slides.text: Brunelleschi probably understood the mathematics but never published it. His friend Leon Battista Alberti did, in De pictura: rays from the eye cross the picture, and similar triangles give how tall a distant thing should look.

slides.heading: The lost proof
slides.text: The panel itself is lost, and no other perspective painting by Brunelleschi is known. We know the experiment mainly from his biographer Antonio Manetti, so exactly how it worked is still debated.

slides.heading: Which of these did Brunelleschi not do?
slides.explanation: Leon Battista Alberti wrote De pictura, about 1435, and credited the discovery to Brunelleschi. Brunelleschi designed the dome, received a patent in 1421 and made the perspective panels.

slides.heading: Match the name to the role
slides.explanation: Brunelleschi demonstrated perspective around 1415–1420, Masaccio painted it in the 1420s, Alberti explained it about 1435, and Manetti told the story.
